content.body:
Kalshi is a New York-based, Commodity Futures Trading Commission-regulated designated contract market that offers event contracts and, increasingly, perpetual futures. Its newest product is a suite of cash-settled perpetual futures tied to more than 50 U.S. stocks, launched Nov. 5. The contracts are subject to CFTC and Securities and Exchange Commission oversight as security futures products. But their legal footing is contested: on Nov. 3, U.S. District Judge Valerie Caproni denied a temporary restraining order sought by the Capital Markets Alliance Association while finding the group was likely to succeed on its argument that the CFTC lacked authority to permit retail single-stock perpetuals. The association’s reply on a preliminary injunction is due Nov. 10.

The larger conflict concerns whether Kalshi’s sports contracts are federally regulated swaps or gambling subject to state law. On Nov. 4, the Ninth Circuit denied rehearing in KalshiEX LLC v. Assad, leaving its Aug. 28 ruling that Nevada may enforce its gaming laws in place; Kalshi has 90 days to seek Supreme Court review. Also on Nov. 4, the Second Circuit declined to block New York and Connecticut enforcement while Kalshi appeals. Arkansas sued Kalshi on Nov. 5, alleging illegal gambling. Utah’s attorney general filed criminal charges on Oct. 28 against KalshiEX and co-founders Tarek Mansour and Luana Lopes Lara, while the Tenth Circuit had declined on Sept. 8 to pause Utah enforcement. Courts remain divided: the Third Circuit protected Kalshi from New Jersey enforcement in April, while the Sixth Circuit allowed Ohio and Tennessee enforcement in September.

The company is expanding beyond binary event contracts on sports, elections, economics, weather, politics and culture. It opened a large-cap U.S. equity-index perpetual future to Kalshi Prime clients on Oct. 7, after launching crypto perpetuals in May and gold and silver contracts in September. Kalshi completed a $1 billion financing at a $40 billion valuation on Oct. 29, led by Sequoia Capital and Wellington Management. Its distribution and data network includes brokerage infrastructure provider Alpaca, institutional block trading through Cantor Fitzgerald, and sports-data agreements with Sportradar. The NBA named Kalshi a preferred prediction-market exchange in October.

Election markets have driven visibility and scrutiny. Kalshi reported more than $1.3 billion in midterm trading before Election Day, and its markets broadly identified the Democratic congressional sweep while missing several consequential races. The exchange added low-volume labels, Brier scores and real-time trade feeds on Oct. 6, and has disciplined users for trading on their own elections or allegedly exploiting nonpublic information. On Oct. 28, it imposed a default $2,500 monthly deposit limit and additional protections for users aged 18 to 20.
